data.text: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile?
data.explanation: CMD sets default commands and arguments that can be overridden from the command line when the container starts. ENTRYPOINT configures the container to run as an executable and cannot be easily overridden (you must use --entrypoint flag). When both are used, CMD provides default arguments to ENTRYPOINT. Best practice: use ENTRYPOINT for the main command and CMD for default arguments.

answers.text: CMD provides defaults that can be overridden; ENTRYPOINT configures the container's main executable
CMD runs at build time; ENTRYPOINT runs at container start
ENTRYPOINT is deprecated in favor of CMD

data.text: What is a Docker volume and why is it used?
data.explanation: Docker volumes are the preferred mechanism for persisting data generated by and used by Docker containers. They are managed by Docker and stored in a part of the host filesystem (/var/lib/docker/volumes/). Unlike bind mounts, volumes are completely managed by Docker, work on both Linux and Windows, can be shared among multiple containers, and support volume drivers for remote storage.

answers.text: A mechanism for persisting data outside the container's writable layer, managed by Docker
A way to increase the container's memory

data.text: What is the difference between COPY and ADD in a Dockerfile?
data.explanation: Both COPY and ADD copy files from the host to the container. However, ADD has additional features: it can extract tar archives automatically and fetch files from remote URLs. Docker best practices recommend using COPY for simple file copying because it's more transparent. Use ADD only when you specifically need tar extraction. For remote URLs, use curl or wget with RUN instead.

answers.text: COPY only copies local files; ADD also supports tar extraction and remote URLs
COPY works with directories; ADD only works with files

data.text: What is a Docker image layer?
data.explanation: Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a read-only layer in the image. Layers are cached and shared between images, which makes builds faster and reduces storage usage. When you change a layer, all subsequent layers must be rebuilt. This is why Dockerfiles should be ordered from least to most frequently changing instructions. The final container adds a thin writable layer on top.

answers.text: A read-only filesystem created by each Dockerfile instruction, cached and shared between images

data.text: Containers share the host OS kernel.
data.explanation: Unlike virtual machines which include a full OS with its own kernel, containers share the host operating system's kernel. They use Linux kernel features like namespaces (for isolation) and cgroups (for resource limits) to create isolated environments. This is why containers are much more lightweight and start faster than VMs, but they must be compatible with the host kernel.
